rows.en: The events after the death of Simeon the Just; Yose ben Yoezer and Yosef ben Yoḥanan; Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes; Yoḥanan the High Priest; Joshua ben Peraḥiah; Nittai of Arbel; Simeon ben Shetaḥ; Judah ben Tabbai; the Kutim [Samaritans]; the victory of the Pharisees; Shemaiah and Avtalyon; the Benei Bathyra.
The events after the death of Simeon the Just.

The first period, which extends from the time of their return from the exile until the end of the Great Assembly, is like a wasteland without a way, which no human foot crosses. Thorns and nettles over the whole of it keep us from going hither and thither. The history of the Torah and of wisdom is wrapped in a thick cloud; only from time to time a small spark of light tears through the clouds, flashes and shines a little, but like lightning it is spent and gone, and in a moment — it is no more. Then the darkness returns, and as at the beginning we grope for the wall like the blind [Isaiah 59:10]. The second period too, toward which we now turn our faces, has not changed its black appearance at its beginning. Although it is plain before our eyes how many were the works of the sages who worked during the time that the Great Assembly lasted, as we perceive the great deeds that suddenly come to light and are seen, nevertheless in darkness it comes and in darkness it goes, and in darkness are covered the names of all the sages who worked and labored on the holy soil [cf. Ecclesiastes 6:4]. And this darkness has stretched out its hands further, from the first period into the second. We have indeed seen the affliction of the people and its distress, which befell it at the hands of Ptolemy I when he went up to Jerusalem and conquered it and multiplied in it mourning and lamentation [Lamentations 2:5]; the days of this king's rule lasted forty years. In the course of these days Onias, son of Jaddua, and after him his son Simeon, called Simeon the Just, stood at the post of the high priesthood (Josephus, *Antiquities* book 12, ch. 2), and in the days of Simeon the Great Assembly ceased. But although the oppression that pressed upon them grew heavy, so that because of it the assembly was abolished, nevertheless it did not find the strength to turn the sages of the Torah away from the goal set before them. The new ideas, too, that the Greeks brought into their land, which found favor in the eyes of the people and spread among them little by little, did not overpower their faith and the teachings of the Torah. Rather the reverse: as the new ideas grew and prospered, so they too girded themselves with strength to hold fast to the Torah and the tradition of their fathers, so that the degenerate shoots of a strange vine [Jeremiah 2:21] should not entwine themselves and climb over them. And as is done with bees — though one guards oneself from their stings, one does not for that reason loathe their honey — so they guarded themselves from the harm of Greek wisdom, but they did not reject it entirely; rather they were sated with its good and planted all that is useful in it in their own soil, so that already in the second half of the first century after the Greeks came to the land of Judah there were in it wise and well-known men who knew Greek wisdom and knew their language and its ways like one of them.

For not many days passed after the death of Ptolemy Lagi, and a new king arose over Egypt [Exodus 1:8], Ptolemy Philadelphus, the son of the first, who did not know the oppression of his father and did not acknowledge his evil. This king did many good things for the benefit of learning, and it was also at his request that the Torah was translated into Greek. According to the testimony of Josephus (*Antiquities* book 12, ch. 2) and Philo (*Life of Moses*), the translators were sages from the land of Israel. The work of translation was done at one time, not piece by piece and book after book; it was made public when it was completed, and the day on which it was completed they made a festival for all generations. Even in the days of Philo the Jews in Alexandria celebrated the day of the deed (Graetz, vol. 3, 478). R. Judah too, in the Talmud (Megillah 9a, and Yerushalmi there), said that our masters permitted writing (the Torah) in Greek; from this it appears that his view is that it was written by the sages of the land of Israel and that our masters permitted the thing. We do not wish to decide that the translation was made in the land of Israel, as the legend has it; but this appears clear: that it was made by sages of Israel and with the consent of the sages in Jerusalem, and that they permitted the translation and its use for every sacred matter. And we cannot imagine their consent without their knowledge of the writing and language of the Greeks and of their wisdom. The legend of seventy or seventy-two elders who translated the Torah is very old. The letter of Aristeas, which contains the story of the translation, already mentions the name "the translation of the Seventy," and surely not long after its appearance it became known by this name. The story of the bringing of seventy-two elders into seventy-two separate places, where each one translated the whole Torah, and that it was a miracle from heaven that all agreed on one meaning (Megillah there, and Josephus),⚠1 is nothing but an aggadah, and one does not learn from aggadah. But the root of the legend, that the translation was made by seventy elders, is true: namely, that the translation was confirmed by the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem and they agreed that it should be used for every sacred matter, as R. Judah and Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel testified (Megillah, Bavli and Yerushalmi, there) that our masters in the land of Israel permitted writing in Greek; and since the number of the Sanhedrin was seventy, they called it the translation of the Seventy. Yet for all that, it is sometimes spoken of with disparagement. The aggadah tells of five elders who wrote the Torah in Greek, and that day was as hard for Israel as the day on which the calf was made (Tractate Soferim ch. 1). This narrator admits that it was made by the sages of Israel, for without doubt he knew the tradition of R. Judah mentioned above, and nevertheless he speaks in disparagement of the translation. This is only because in changing times opinions changed regarding the study of Greek wisdom. The opinions of his time overpowered this narrator himself, for in his time perhaps the ancient decree from the days of the Hasmoneans was in force, which was redoubled at a later time, that one must not study Greek wisdom, as will be made clear further below; and therefore the translation was displeasing to him. But against this it is related of Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel (Yerushalmi Megillah ch. 1) that when the sages permitted writing the Torah in Greek, they examined and found that the Torah can be translated adequately only into Greek. This is because R. Simeon was one of the sages who loved the Greek language and their wisdom, as all the patriarchs from Hillel onward loved it, and therefore his mouth was full of praise and glory for the Greek translation. And perhaps for another reason as well some sages disparaged this translation, because it translates according to the plain sense and paid no heed to the Oral Torah; and therefore the later ones said the opposite of the words of R. Simeon. He used to say that they examined and found that the Torah can be translated adequately only into Greek, and they said that the Torah cannot be translated adequately, because the translation does not heed the interpretations of the Oral Torah, and in their view any translation that is not according to the interpretations is not an adequate translation.

1.note: Josephus (Antiquities 12.2) tells of the 72 elders but not of the separate places and the miracle; reference kept as printed.

rows.en: If we pay attention to the periods of ancient times, we will find that opinions about the Septuagint changed from time to time. At first their mouth was full of praise and glory for it, for in the work of translation they saw that honor was given to the Torah, and in the honor of the Torah they saw their own honor; and at that time the Jews did not begrudge any other wisdom, but honored all wisdom. Opinions reached another stage from the time when the interpretations of the Oral Torah were fruitful and multiplied; from then on many disparaged the Greek translation. To this the aggadah alludes: "Moses asked that the Mishnah too should be in writing, but because the Holy One, blessed be He, foresaw that the nations of the world would in future translate the Torah and read it in Greek, and they would say, 'We are Israel' .... The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: You say that you are My children; I know only the one who has My mysteries with him. And which is that? It is the Mishnah, which was given orally" (Tanḥuma and Exodus Rabbah, portion Ki Tissa, and in many places). The idea of this aggadah is to disparage the Greek translation, because in it all the fine points of the Torah and the fine points of the Scribes, which are the substance of the Oral Torah, are impossible. At a still later time they rejected it altogether because of the heretics; for the heretics disputed with Israel over words of Torah, and also other scholars from among the sages of the nations reproached them and opposed the teachings of the Torah, such as the gentile sage Celsus, against whom the Christian Origen stood up. And who brought both of these into the secret of the Torah if not the Greek translation? Therefore it was as thorns in the eyes of the Jews.{v1_06_03:1} So indeed it was in ancient days. But times have changed, and with them our opinions on this matter too. Through the Septuagint the springs of the wisdom of the Torah were opened to the nations as well, and the prophecies of our prophets and the wisdom of our sages became known to them; and it was almost the means that helps us to fulfil our mission in the world according to the promises of the prophets: to bring the knowledge of one God to all the peoples besides us. We have no reason to disparage this translation any more, but rather to praise and glorify it, as did the ancients, the sages of that generation in the land of Israel, who were pleased with it when it appeared and approved it. It is true that in one respect this translation did harm in recent times too, for some interpreters of Scripture, on its basis, laid hands on our holy writings and emended them and spoiled their pleasant words, saying that according to the translation the translators had such-and-such a reading before them, not like our reading. But this is not the fault of the translation; it is the fault of those emenders, who did not consider the matter with faithful care and did not think that perhaps the error is in the translation and not in the text of Scripture, or that perhaps the translator translated and altered for the sake of a clearer explanation and turned aside from the main reading, as Onkelos did in his translation — according to the statement of Menaḥem ben Saruq in the *Maḥberet* (entry eitan) — that he came only to broaden the explanation so that it would sit well; and especially since it is known that busy hands have touched this translation and corrupted it, deliberately or by mistake, from some other motive or unknowingly.

Now, after we have seen that this translation, made in the days of Ptolemy Philadelphus, came from the hands of the sages of Israel and that our masters approved it,{v1_06_03:2} we understand why in several places in this translation there are clear traces of words of tradition. And even though the hands of falsifiers have touched the Septuagint that is before us, nevertheless everything in it that agrees with the tradition testifies of itself that it is original, as it came from the hands of the first translators, and that neither the hands of falsifiers nor the lying pen of scribes [Jeremiah 8:8] have touched it. The Jews in the land of Israel were never suspected of falsifying the translation, for it was not in their hands; and the Alexandrian Jews, had they been falsifiers, would not have done so for the benefit of the midrash of the sages of the land of Israel; and all the more so other falsifiers, who do not believe in the tradition and in the interpretations of the sages, would not falsify and alter the translation so that it would agree with the tradition. Therefore what is found in this translation in agreement with the tradition certainly came from the hands of the first translators and is the interpretation received from of old. For example, their translation of "on the morrow of the Sabbath" [Leviticus 23:11], said of the offering of the omer, which they interpret as the day after the first day of the festival of unleavened bread; this agrees with the interpretation of the Talmudic sages (Menaḥot 65a). Likewise they translated "and has no son," said in the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5), as if it were written "and has no seed," and this too agrees with the halakhah that a daughter also exempts from levirate marriage. Moreover, they sometimes added words in their translation to agree with the halakhah. "And the master of the house shall come near to God" (Exodus 22:6),⚠1 said in the law of the bailees, they interpreted to mean that coming near to God is that he shall come near to God to confirm his word by an oath, and they added the word "and he shall swear"; this agrees with the interpretation of the rabbis (Mekhilta Mishpatim ch. 15, and in the Gemara in many places), who also interpreted it as an oath.{v1_06_04:1} Thus it follows for us that there are in the Septuagint interpretations that the translators gave according to the tradition and according to the well-known halakhah, and they interpreted so wherever the way of translation and its purpose would bear it, that is, where it does not need an expansion of words if one wishes to translate according to the received interpretation. Now, when we find in it translations that are opposed to the interpretations of the Oral Torah, we cannot judge from this that at the time it was made those interpretations were not yet known. Only in a case where, had he wished to translate according to the interpretation of the Oral Torah, he would not have needed to expand the words — then we will say: had the interpretation been known in their time, they would surely have put it into their translation, as they put in other interpretations of this kind, as we have seen. But if he would have needed to expand the words, then we will say: even if he did not translate in agreement with the interpretation of the Oral Torah, this is still no proof that that interpretation was not known in their time; for it is possible that it was known and nevertheless he did not use it, since the task of the translator is only to carry the words of the book he translates over into the language into which he translates, not to expand the words with interpretations, by which he would be forced to add many more words than the words of the translated book. Therefore, if we find in the Septuagint that it translated "an eye for an eye" [Exodus 21:24] according to its plain sense and its wording, and not according to the interpretation of the Oral Torah, which explained this verse as monetary compensation, this is no proof that the interpretation of the halakhah was not yet known, for we will say that he refrained from translating according to the received interpretation because he would have needed to expand the words, and this is against the purpose of the translator. But from what is found in the Septuagint, that it translated "as he had schemed to do to his brother" [Deuteronomy 19:19] as if it were written "as he had wickedly sought to do to his brother," explaining zamam in the sense of zimmah [wickedness], from this there is certainly proof that it did not interpret according to the interpretation of the halakhah, which explained that they are punished only for the intention, and if they have killed they are not put to death. And although this halakhah is not clearly from the tradition, and in our opinion the truth is that according to the tradition they are put to death even if they have killed, only that they are punished for the intention as well; at any rate, according to the translation it appears that its intention is that there is punishment only for the deed, not for the intention.

1.note: The verse is Exodus 22:7 in the Hebrew numbering; kept as printed.

rows.en: This Greek translation was used by the Jews living in Alexandria and by those living in the cities on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, the cities in which the Greeks had settled and the Jews lived among them. From of old there was an ordinance in Israel to read portions of the Torah when they gathered together for the service of the Lord. It was also the custom that men of understanding translated the Torah into Aramaic, the language understood by the mass of the people. Therefore, for the purpose of this reading, which was ancient, and for the purpose of instruction in the Torah of the Lord, the Torah was written in Greek in Alexandria. But a doubt arose: was this Greek translation proper according to the religion, to read from it to fulfil the obligation of the reading? This question was put to the rabbis in the land of Israel, and they permitted the thing. This follows explicitly from the account of R. Judah, who relates that our masters permitted Greek because of the incident of King Ptolemy (Megillah 9a). The sages examined and found that the Torah can be translated adequately only into Greek (Yerushalmi there). From this it appears that the sages confirmed the translation, and by their will the permission went forth to write the Torah in Greek and to use it for every sacred matter. On the basis of this permission it came about in practice that the study of the Torah and the public reading were all in the Greek language, so that within a short time they had no Hebrew copy, for they did not need it and did not understand it. The grandson of Joshua ben Sira (about one hundred and forty years before the Christian era) testified in the preface to his Greek translation of his grandfather's book that when he stayed in Alexandria he found that the Alexandrian Jews differed greatly in their spiritual character from their brethren in the land of Israel; and not only is there a great difference between the one and the other with regard to the Holy Scriptures, but there is also a difference between them in their understanding of them. And what was this difference between them with regard to the Holy Scriptures? It is only that the Jews in the land of Israel had the Holy Scriptures in their own language, which is Hebrew, while in Alexandria they had only a Greek translation. At that time, when the sages saw the need to publish their ruling concerning the reading of the Torah in the Greek translation, surely at the same period they also decided the law regarding the various portions of the Torah that by statute and custom were fixed to be recited, such as the portion of the suspected wife, the declaration of the tithe, and the reading of the Shema. Likewise the question arose concerning the fixed prayer and the grace after meals: is there in all these any strictness as to the language in which they are said? And a halakhah dealing with these matters has also been preserved for us (Sotah 7:1): "These are said in any language: the portion of the suspected wife, the declaration of the tithe, the reading of the Shema, the prayer, the grace after meals, the oath of testimony and the oath of deposit." It is very likely that at the time when they permitted Greek because of the incident of King Ptolemy, this halakhah too was newly made. And although the sages of the generation already had great reason to speak of this at the beginning of the days of the Scribes, since already then there were many who understood only Aramaic, nevertheless it appears from the language of the Mishnah that it is aimed at other languages; for in saying "these are said in any language" it hints that it speaks of yet another language besides Aramaic. And which is it? It is Greek. This deficiency in knowledge of Hebrew grew very strong in Alexandria, and it came upon them from their mingling with the Greeks, the inhabitants of the land. And the same happened to them in all the places in which the Greeks had settled, and especially in the cities on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea. Those places were called by the general name "the province of the sea" (*Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, gate 12). And since they knew in the land of Israel that the Jews living in those provinces were not expert in matters of religion and in the fine points of the laws, by the measure of the land of Israel, and also on account of their levity they were not trusted by the sages of the land of Israel in several matters touching religion, they therefore prepared and also founded a new ordinance (Gittin 1:1): that every agent who brings a bill of divorce from the province of the sea must say "It was written in my presence and signed in my presence." For in any case there were fixed courts in those provinces; and even if at a later time it was not so, nevertheless at first there were fixed courts in Alexandria (Tosefta Pe'ah ch. 4, Ketubbot ch. 3, and Bavli there 25a),{v1_06_05:1} and this was at a time when they still clung strongly to the religion of their fathers. Therefore, if the agent said that the bill was written and signed in his presence, they knew whether it had been written according to its law, for he could tell them whether it had been done in a court or not (see Gittin 2b, and Rashi's commentary). And although a bill of divorce need not be given before a court, at any rate it must be made under the direction of an expert; therefore a court is needed when it is made in a province whose people know nothing of the matters of the Torah and its fine points. And perhaps this itself was included in the ordinance: not to rely on a bill of divorce that was not made in a court of experts. Such an ordinance was necessary for another reason too: since the language used by the inhabitants of these provinces was Greek, and this language was not understood by every court in the land of Israel, they therefore ordained that at any rate the agent who brings a bill of divorce from these provinces should testify — for without doubt it was written in their language — to the truth of the writing of the bill and of its signing in a court of experts. This was the foundation of the ordinance in the first place; but at a later time its foundation and its reason were already forgotten, so that the sages of the Talmud were already in doubt about its reason and the grounds of its foundation.{v1_06_06:1}

footnotes.en: Rav Sherira Gaon, in his letter to the community of Kairouan printed in *Yuḥasin*, wrote in several places that Rabbi wrote down the Mishnah, and Maimonides followed him in his introduction to the Mishnah. Regarding the writing of the Mishnah in particular, we will speak further in the proper place. R. Jacob Ḥagiz, in the introduction to his commentary on the Mishnah *Etz Ḥayyim*, wrote at great length and brings proofs to uphold the words of Rashi, who said in several places in the Talmud that they did not write anything of the Oral Torah. R. Samuel David Luzzatto held this view in *Kerem Ḥemed* vol. 3, and likewise R. Hirsch Chajes in his work *Mevo ha-Talmud*; but all their words are built on shaky foundations. R. Zacharias Frankel, in *Darkhei ha-Mishnah* p. 217, wrote sensible and reliable words on this matter and decided according to the view of Rav Sherira Gaon. The scholar Lebrecht, in his work *Kritische Lese* p. 12, also wrote decisively that they wrote down oral matters, and the words were repeated in the work *Wissenschaftliche Blätter* p. 3. See further what I wrote in the introduction to the Sifra printed in Vienna in the year [5]625⚠1 with the commentary of Rabad and with my work *Masoret ha-Talmud*. There will be further occasion to speak of this matter in this work; see below in this volume ch. 22, and in vol. 2 ch. 13 and there ch. 22; and I treated the subject at length in vol. 3 ch. 20, and see there vol. 4⚠2 p. 164 and in the note no. 4. See also above, ch. 2, in the note where I conjectured that according to R. Judah, who said that Joshua wrote the portion of the cities of refuge as a teaching he received from Moses orally, Joshua would be the first who wrote down oral matters.

footnotes.en: These words, from the passage beginning "If we pay attention" up to "in the eyes of the Jews," I heard from my friend Dr. Aaron Jellinek in his sermons in our house of study; and because they were very right in my eyes, I have set them before my readers, and may their soul delight in them.

Graetz, vol. 3 p. 478, decides that the translation was made in the days of Philometor, about a hundred years after Ptolemy Philadelphus. But in all the inquiries and investigations of the various critics on this subject, nothing clear has been found that is not contradicted from another place. Yet among most of them, from what I have seen, there is agreement on the main point, namely that the translation came into being in the time of Philadelphus; this view satisfied my mind and I followed it. And in his book on the Septuagint R. Zacharias Frankel brought most of the opinions of the Christian authors on this side.

On the matters in which the Septuagint agrees with the tradition, see the books of R. Zacharias Frankel: *Darkhei ha-Mishnah* p. 11 and p. 314, his book on the translation, and the book *Mi-Midrash ha-Aleksandronim*⚠1.

footnotes.en: In the Bavli, Ketubbot, the reading is "formerly, when there were fixed courts in Alexandria." Such is the reading also in the Tosefta of Pe'ah and of Ketubbot, and from this it appears that they referred to an early time. But in Yerushalmi Ketubbot ch. 1 I found this reading: "even in Alexandria, at the time when the courts sit." The difference between the two readings is that according to the Bavli and the Tosefta there was a fixed court only in an early time, and it ceased afterward and was no more; while according to the reading of the Yerushalmi there were times when there was a court and times when they ceased.
